title: Self-Study Reconsidered: The Hidden Fragility of Learning from Self-Generated QA
summary: Language models are increasingly taught from synthetic question--answer (QA) supervision: a model generates questions about a document, answers them from the same text, and the resulting pairs are used to fine-tune, distill, or compress knowledge into another model. We show that this generation step is not neutral preprocessing. It is an implicit policy that both selects which evidence becomes training signal and decides how that evidence is answered, and it is fragile at both stages. When choosing what to ask, generators do not scan a document uniformly. Coverage saturates early and concentrates on salient spans, diverse prompts converge on the same regions, and what looks question-worthy is driven by local presentation. As a result, salient artifacts such as poorly cleaned markup can hijack question generation across model families and scales. When answering, the model that produces the supervision tends to obey instruction-like passages embedded in the text. This compliance depends on the intent and surface form of the passage rather than its strictness, and is worst under task conflict, where larger models comply more often. These failure modes arise from choices made during QA generation, so they can be reduced without changing the training loop. Tying each question to a fixed target reduces biased selection, and filtering instruction-like spans before answering lowers mean injection compliance from $88\%$ to $13\%$ in our evaluation while retaining nearly all clean text.

AI.tldr: Synthetic QA supervision from language models has two hidden biases: (1) question generation is non-uniform, easily hijacked by surface features like markup; (2) answer generation makes models comply with instruction-like text passages, which scales with model size. Simple preprocessing fixes (fixed targets and span filtering) reduce these biases dramatically.
AI.motivation: Synthetic QA data is widely used for fine-tuning, distillation, and knowledge compression, but the assumption that QA generation is neutral preprocessing is questionable. The authors aim to uncover and quantify hidden biases in this process.
AI.method: The authors systematically analyze two stages of QA generation: (1) question selection—measuring coverage saturation, salience concentration, prompt convergence, and vulnerability to markup artifacts across model families/scales; (2) answer compliance—testing how models obey instruction-like passages embedded in text, varying intent, surface form, strictness, and task conflict, with scaling analysis. They then propose two mitigation strategies: fixed-target tying and instruction-like span filtering.
AI.result: Question coverage saturates early and concentrates on salient spans; diverse prompts yield similar regions; markup artifacts hijack generation across models. Answer generators comply with instruction-like passages (88% injection rate), especially under task conflict, with larger models more compliant. Mitigation reduces compliance from 88% to 13% while retaining clean text.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic QA supervision is not neutral; it encodes systematic biases at both the question-selection and answer-generation stages. These can be mitigated via simple preprocessing interventions without modifying the training loop, making synthetic data more reliable.

title: PolicyGuard: From Organizational Policies to Neuro-SymbolicCompliance Review Engines
summary: Policy-grounded document review requires determining whether a target document complies with organization-specific policies, guidelines, or playbooks. While large language models can assist with policy interpretation and document analysis, end-to-end prompting leaves the applied policy logic implicit, making compliance decisions difficult to inspect, update, and test. We present PolicyGuard, a neuro-symbolic framework for policy-grounded document compliance review. PolicyGuard converts organizational policy guidance into an executable review engine consisting of typed relational logic rules and atom-level extraction questions. During review, LLMs answer these local questions using retrieved document evidence, and a symbolic evaluator applies the formal rules to detect non-compliance. We instantiate and evaluate PolicyGuard on company-specific NDA compliance review, where contract clauses must be checked against organization-specific negotiation policies. By separating policy formalization, local document interpretation, and symbolic compliance evaluation, PolicyGuard makes document review more explicit, maintainable, and systematically testable.

AI.tldr: PolicyGuard is a neuro-symbolic framework that converts organizational policies into executable rules and local extraction questions, using LLMs to answer questions with evidence and symbolic evaluation to detect non-compliance, demonstrated on NDA compliance review.
AI.motivation: End-to-end LLM prompting for policy-grounded document review leaves policy logic implicit, making compliance decisions difficult to inspect, update, and test. A more explicit and maintainable approach is needed.
AI.method: PolicyGuard converts policies into typed relational logic rules and atom-level extraction questions; LLMs answer local questions with retrieved evidence; a symbolic evaluator applies formal rules to detect non-compliance.
AI.result: Instantiated and evaluated on company-specific NDA compliance review, where contract clauses are checked against negotiation policies.
AI.conclusion: By separating policy formalization, local document interpretation, and symbolic compliance evaluation, PolicyGuard makes document review more explicit, maintainable, and systematically testable.

title: AxDafny: Agentic Verified Code Generation in Dafny
summary: We study agentic code generation in Dafny, where a model must generate both executable code and the proof artifacts for verification. We present AxDafny, a verifier-guided repair framework that iteratively generates implementations, invariants, assertions, and termination arguments. We also introduce LiveCodeBench-Pro-Dafny (LCB-Pro-Dafny), a benchmark of 250 competition-style programming problems translated into Dafny with formal specifications and a verifier-based evaluation harness. On LCB-Pro-Dafny, AxDafny substantially improves verification success over baseline GPT-5.5 performance. On DafnyBench, AxDafny achieves 92.7\% verification success, outperforming the strongest previously reported proof-hint baseline by 6.5 percentage points. Lastly, we show that verification success and runtime test performance measure different aspects of generated code.

AI.tldr: AxDafny is a verifier-guided repair framework for agentic code generation in Dafny that iteratively generates code and proof artifacts. It introduces LCB-Pro-Dafny benchmark and achieves 92.7% verification success on DafnyBench, outperforming prior work by 6.5 percentage points. The paper also shows verification success and runtime tests measure different code aspects.
AI.motivation: To enable LLMs to generate both executable code and formal proof artifacts for verification in Dafny, addressing the challenge of producing correct-by-construction programs with machine-checkable proofs.
AI.method: AxDafny uses a verifier-guided repair loop that iteratively generates implementations, invariants, assertions, and termination arguments, guided by feedback from the Dafny verifier.
AI.result: On LCB-Pro-Dafny, AxDafny improves verification success over baseline GPT-5.5. On DafnyBench, it achieves 92.7% verification success, outperforming the best prior proof-hint baseline by 6.5 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Verification success and runtime test performance capture different aspects of generated code, suggesting both are needed for comprehensive evaluation of code generation.
